overview.text: Giuseppe Garibaldi was a military leader in the nineteenth-century movement to unify Italy, known as the Risorgimento. In 1860 he led a volunteer expedition from Quarto to Sicily, then part of the Bourbon-ruled Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. His followers, remembered as Red Shirts, won battles on the island and continued onto the mainland. Garibaldi entered Naples in September and governed territory captured from the Bourbons. Rather than establish a separate state, he supported Victor Emmanuel II as king of a united Italy. The campaign helped bring southern Italy into the kingdom proclaimed in 1861, although unification continued afterward.

The Red Shirts were volunteers associated with Garibaldi's campaign.

A plebiscite in October 1860 endorsed annexation of the former Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

overview.text: The Chernobyl disaster began on 26 April 1986 at reactor four of a nuclear power plant in Soviet Ukraine. During a test of how the unit would supply power in an emergency, the reactor became unstable; explosions and a fire destroyed its core and released radioactive material. An International Atomic Energy Agency investigation identified both reactor-design deficiencies and actions by plant personnel as important to understanding the accident. Wind carried radioactive fallout across parts of Ukraine, Belarus, Russia, and beyond. Authorities evacuated nearby Pripyat and other settlements, while workers undertook cleanup and containment. Chernobyl became a major case study in nuclear safety and the long social costs of disaster.

overview.text: Russia's Time of Troubles was a period of dynastic and political crisis usually dated from 1598 to 1613. It began after Tsar Fedor died without an heir, ending the hereditary Rurikid line. Boris Godunov was chosen as ruler, but famine, rebellion, and rival claimants weakened the state. A pretender known as False Dmitry gained power with Polish support, and Polish forces later occupied Moscow. A militia associated with Kuzma Minin and Dmitry Pozharsky helped expel them in 1612. The election of Michael Romanov as tsar in 1613 began a new ruling dynasty, although war and instability did not vanish immediately.

overview.text: Thailand is a Southeast Asian kingdom formerly known internationally as Siam. Its history includes the kingdom centered on Ayutthaya, founded around 1350 after Sukhothai and linked to far-reaching trade and diplomacy. Burmese forces destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767; Bangkok later became the capital of a reconstituted Siamese kingdom. In June 1932, a group of civilian and military reformers called the People's Party ended absolute monarchy through a coup, establishing a constitutional monarchy. The country adopted the name Thailand in 1939. These changes show why Siam and Thailand refer to different periods of the same country's history, rather than two unrelated states.

overview.text: Sea Peoples is a modern label for several groups mentioned in Egyptian accounts of conflicts around the eastern Mediterranean near the end of the Bronze Age. Egyptian inscriptions describe battles under pharaohs Merenptah and Ramesses III, including fighting by land and sea near the Nile Delta. The sources name groups such as the Peleset, Shekelesh, and Sherden. Their precise homelands and relationships remain debated, so the label should not suggest a single nation with one clear origin. The upheavals of this era involved movement and conflict across a wider region, not one simple invasion story.

key_facts.text: The Sea Peoples were several named groups, not one clearly identified nation.
Egyptian records connect them with conflicts under Merenptah and Ramesses III.
Ramesses III recorded fighting them at Medinet Habu.
Peleset, Shekelesh, and Sherden are names recorded in Egyptian sources.
The groups' movements included routes by land and sea.

overview.text: James VI and I was king of Scotland as James VI and later king of England as James I. He became Scotland's monarch as an infant in 1567 and inherited England's crown in 1603 after Elizabeth I died. The two kingdoms shared a ruler, but his proposed full political union did not take effect. James commissioned a new English Bible translation, remembered as the King James or Authorized Version. His reign also saw the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605 and repeated disputes with Parliament about money and royal authority. He died in 1625 and was succeeded in England by his son Charles I.

key_facts.text: James became king of Scotland in 1567, while still an infant.
He inherited England's throne in 1603 after Elizabeth I.
His attempt at full governmental union of England and Scotland did not succeed.
James commissioned the Authorized, or King James, Bible translation.

overview.text: La Noche Triste, or the Night of Sorrows, names the defeat of Hernán Cortés's forces while they tried to leave the Mexica capital Tenochtitlan around the night of 30 June 1520. Spanish soldiers and their Indigenous allies attempted to escape along the Tacuba causeway. Mexica fighters discovered them and attacked from the causeway and the lake, causing heavy losses and the loss of horses, weapons, and captured gold. The Spanish name emphasizes Cortés's defeat; for the Mexica it was a victory. Cortés survived, regrouped with allies in Tlaxcala, and later returned to besiege Tenochtitlan in 1521.

Cortés's forces tried to flee by the Tacuba causeway.
Mexica fighters attacked on land and from the lake.
Spanish and Tlaxcalan fighters both suffered losses.

overview.text: Wu Zetian rose from the Tang imperial court to rule China as emperor in her own right. Her reign as emperor lasted from 690 to 705 CE, when she used the dynastic name Zhou, interrupting the Tang line. She is distinguished from earlier and later empresses because she formally held the imperial title herself. Her rule was connected to Luoyang and to Buddhist institutions and imagery. A surviving inscription dated 703 records a Buddhist shrine built to pray for her health, giving historians material evidence of court religious patronage. After her rule, the Tang dynasty continued. Her career challenges the assumption that imperial China never had a woman emperor.

overview.text: Wool is an animal fiber used to make textiles, especially from the fleece of sheep. Its fibers contain keratin, a protein also found in hair and nails. Their natural waviness helps trap air, making wool useful for warm clothing and blankets. People have used animal wool for textiles across many regions and centuries, from garments to rugs. To weave it, workers spin shorter fibers into yarn; the overlapping scales on wool fibers also let them bind together as felt. Fiber thickness varies by breed and body area, so some wool suits soft clothing while coarser types suit sturdier goods. Wool also became an important traded material.

overview.text: The Netherlands is a country in northwestern Europe whose earlier history includes the Dutch Republic. That republic joined seven provinces for common defense and foreign policy while preserving local autonomy. It gave way to other states during the French revolutionary era, and the modern Kingdom of the Netherlands emerged in 1815. Dutch merchants also built overseas trading networks; the Dutch East India Company, or VOC, established a colonial system in Indonesia and used force to secure some commodities. Seventeenth-century Dutch wealth supported art and urban building, including work by Rembrandt and Vermeer. Today the wider Kingdom also includes Aruba, Curaçao, and St Maarten as constituent countries.
